cards.front: Why must safe driving in bad weather and emergencies be studied?
cards.back: Most drivers learn under normal conditions, so safe driving in changing weather, light or emergencies must be learned through study and experience.
cards.memory_hook: learned in normal, study the rest

cards.front: About how many of Alabama's fatal crashes happen in darkness?
cards.back: About half of Alabama's fatal crashes happen during darkness, even though traffic is light then.

cards.front: What does it mean not to overdrive your headlights?
cards.back: Never overdrive your headlights: keep a speed at which you can stop within the distance your lights show ahead.

cards.front: How far do high beams usually light the road?
cards.back: Under normal conditions, high beams usually light the road about three hundred fifty feet ahead.

cards.front: How close to other vehicles must you dim your headlights?
cards.back: The law requires dimming your headlights within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle and within two hundred feet of a vehicle you are following.
cards.memory_hook: five hundred meeting, two hundred following

cards.front: What if an oncoming driver keeps high beams on after you dim?
cards.back: If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on after you dim, keep yours dimmed anyway, since blinding that driver only endangers you.

cards.front: What should you keep clean and clear for night driving?
cards.back: Keep lights working and lenses clean, and keep all vehicle glass clean, free of defects and clear of frost and steam.

cards.front: When does state law require headlights?
cards.back: State law requires headlights, not just parking lights, starting a half-hour after sunset and lasting until a half-hour before sunrise, and also whenever you cannot see clearly for at least five hundred feet.

cards.front: What should you do if you are unsure whether lights are needed?
cards.back: When unsure whether lights are needed, turn them on low beam, which helps you see and helps others see you.

cards.front: What should you watch for at night, and what should you study ahead?
cards.back: At night watch closely for signs, pedestrians, bicycles, slow vehicles and animals, and study maps ahead of time.

cards.front: How can a companion and your eye habits help at night?
cards.back: A companion can act as a second pair of eyes for signs and hazards, and moving your eyes from near to far and side to side eases night eye fatigue.

cards.front: How do the dimming distances compare with the visibility distance for headlights?
cards.back: Dim within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic and within two hundred feet behind a car, while headlights are required whenever you cannot see five hundred feet ahead.
cards.memory_hook: five hundred, two hundred, five hundred

cards.front: How do you cut glare from oncoming headlights?
cards.back: To cut glare from oncoming lights, look away toward the right edge of the pavement and its white line.

cards.front: How do you handle glare from headlights behind you?
cards.back: For glare from behind, use a day-night mirror or adjust the mirror to block most of the light.

cards.front: What should you do if your car breaks down at night?
cards.back: In a night breakdown, pull well off the road, turn on four-way flashers, raise the hood, and stay with the car if you can.

cards.front: If you must walk after a night breakdown, how do you walk and where do flares go?
cards.back: If you must walk, carry a light and walk on the left edge facing traffic, and place flares or reflectors one hundred to five hundred feet behind the car on the right edge.

cards.front: Why is speed more dangerous at night?
cards.back: Speed is more dangerous at night because at high speed your headlight range does not give enough stopping distance, so obey limits even on roads you know.

cards.front: What does winter add, and is bad weather usually to blame for crashes?
cards.back: Winter adds darkness, fog, rain, snow, sleet and ice, and in most cases bad weather alone cannot be blamed for crashes.

cards.front: What should you do before driving in winter?
cards.back: Warm the engine while clearing snow and ice from the car and windows, and keep washer fluid mixed with anti-freeze.

cards.front: Why avoid using washers at high speed in extreme cold?
cards.back: In extreme cold, avoid using washers at high speed, since the fluid can freeze on the glass and block your view.

cards.front: How do you find out how slippery the road is?
cards.back: Test your brakes gently at low speed to learn how slippery the road is, then set your speed to match.

cards.front: What do snow treads do, and do they let you drive normally?
cards.back: Snow treads on the drive wheels improve traction in snow, but you still drive below normal speed and leave more stopping room.

cards.front: What is best for severe ice or very deep snow?
cards.back: Snow treads do not grip ice; for severe ice, hard-packed snow or very deep snow, reinforced tire chains are best.

cards.front: When does Alabama law require headlights with wipers?
cards.back: Alabama law requires headlights whenever wipers are running for rain, sleet or snow, but intermittent wiper use does not require them.

cards.front: How much farther does it take to stop on snow or ice?
cards.back: On snow or ice a car needs three to twelve times the stopping distance it needs on dry pavement, so keep well back.

cards.front: How do you start moving on snow or ice?
cards.back: To start on snow or ice, keep engine speed very low; with a clutch release it slowly or use second or high gear, and with an automatic accelerate gently.

cards.front: How do you brake on packed snow or ice?
cards.back: On packed snow or ice brake gently, and for a sudden stop pump the brakes, easing off whenever the wheels lock or start to slip, without pushing in the clutch.

cards.front: What happens in a skid?
cards.back: A skid happens when the tires lose their grip, and then the engine, brakes and even steering lose effect.

cards.front: Should you brake during a skid?
cards.back: Do not brake in a skid until you regain your forward direction, since braking speeds the skid and locked front wheels lose steering.

cards.front: How do you recover from a skid in a rear-wheel drive car?
cards.back: To end a skid, keep the rear from outrunning the front; in a rear-wheel drive car, easing off the gas slows the rear wheels and, with steering, straightens the car.

cards.front: How do you recover from a skid in a front-wheel drive car?
cards.back: In a front-wheel drive car, a light touch on the gas speeds the front wheels so the front catches up and the skid straightens.

cards.front: What is the next best step if there is no room to accelerate in a skid?
cards.back: Without room to accelerate, the next best step is to disengage the transmission and steer the way the rear is skidding, though many experts warn against shifting to neutral in a panic.

cards.front: At what speeds does hydroplaning start and become total in a standard car?
cards.back: On wet roads most tires wipe the surface up to thirty-five miles per hour, but in a standard car partial hydroplaning starts near thirty-five miles per hour and can become total near fifty-five miles per hour

cards.front: What happens during total hydroplaning?
cards.back: With total hydroplaning there is no friction to brake, speed up or turn, so wind or a slight curve can cause an uncontrollable skid.

cards.front: What should you do if you hydroplane?
cards.back: If you hydroplane, take your foot off the accelerator; correct a partial-hydroplane skid, but in a total one just release the gas and ride it out.

cards.front: How do tires affect hydroplaning, and when is complete hydroplaning expected?
cards.back: Good tires with deep tread help prevent hydroplaning, but when water is deeper than the tread, expect complete hydroplaning above fifty miles per hour

decks.domain: Adjusting to driving conditions (fog, hills, carbon monoxide, emergencies, confusables)

cards.front: How should you drive in fog or a snowstorm?
cards.back: Avoid driving in fog or a snowstorm unless absolutely necessary, and when visibility is limited, slow down enough to stop within the distance you can see.

cards.front: Which beams should you use in fog or heavy snow?
cards.back: Use low beams in fog or heavy snow to cut the glare thrown back at you.

cards.front: What should you do if you cannot see in fog?
cards.back: If you cannot see, or tire from straining to see, pull fully off the road, leave the lights on, park and wait for better visibility.

cards.front: Why use extra caution on narrow hilly roads?
cards.back: Narrow hilly or wooded roads hide blind pockets where another car may be only feet away before you see it, so use extra caution and tap the horn on dangerous curves.

cards.front: May you coast downhill in neutral?
cards.back: The law forbids coasting downhill with the transmission in neutral.

cards.front: When is carbon monoxide poisoning more likely, and why is it dangerous?
cards.back: Carbon monoxide poisoning is likelier in winter, when windows stay shut and engines are warmed up, and the fumes have no odor and can kill.

cards.front: What are the signs of carbon monoxide poisoning, and what is the cure?
cards.back: Sudden weariness, yawning, dizziness and nausea signal carbon monoxide poisoning, and the only cure is plenty of fresh air.

cards.front: How do you prevent carbon monoxide poisoning?
cards.back: Prevent it by having the exhaust checked for leaks, not idling or driving with windows shut tight, and never warming up in a closed garage.

decks.domain: Adjusting to driving conditions (fog, hills, carbon monoxide, emergencies, confusables)

cards.front: What is the basic rule in any driving emergency?
cards.back: In any emergency, think before you act, since instinct, like slamming the brakes in a skid, can be the wrong move.

cards.front: What should you do after a blowout?
cards.back: After a blowout, grip the wheel, steer straight, ease off the gas and do not brake until the car is under control; a thumping bulge can warn of one.

cards.front: What commonly causes blowouts, and what does fast air loss do?
cards.back: Under-inflation is one of the most common causes of blowouts, and a tire losing air fast pulls the car to one side.

cards.front: How do you respond to losing a wheel?
cards.back: Losing a wheel gives the same warnings and needs the same response as a blowout: hold tight, steer straight, ease off the gas, no braking until slowed and in control.

cards.front: What should you do if your steering fails?
cards.back: If steering fails, ease off the gas without braking or shifting, then brake very gently once the car has slowed.

cards.front: What should you do if the brake pedal sinks to the floor?
cards.back: If the brake pedal sinks to the floor, pump it; a spongy, slowly sinking pedal is the usual early warning of brake failure.

cards.front: What can you do if pumping the brakes does not work?
cards.back: If pumping fails, apply the parking brake gently to avoid a skid, shift to a lower gear, or switch off the engine in gear, knowing power steering and brakes then stop assisting.

cards.front: Which failures call for easing off the gas instead of braking hard?
cards.back: A blowout, a lost wheel and a steering failure all call for easing off the gas instead of braking hard.

decks.domain: Adjusting to driving conditions (fog, hills, carbon monoxide, emergencies, confusables)

cards.front: What should you do if your wheels drop onto the shoulder?
cards.back: If your wheels drop onto the shoulder, do not swerve back; stay on it, slow down, then ease gently back onto the pavement.

cards.front: What should you do if a car comes at you in your lane?
cards.back: If a car comes at you in your lane, pull right, slow down, sound the horn or flash lights at night, and never swerve into the left lane.

cards.front: How can you help a passing car that is stuck beside you?
cards.back: If a passing car is stuck beside you, slow down when it can still get ahead, speed up when it must drop back, and move onto a good shoulder if a crash is nearly certain.

cards.front: How might you move a car stalled on the tracks?
cards.back: A stalled manual car may be moved off tracks by running the starter in low or second gear, but an automatic has to be pushed.

cards.front: If a train is coming and your car will not move, what should you do?
cards.back: If a train is coming and the car will not move, leave it and walk beside the tracks toward the train so debris from the impact will not hit you.

cards.front: If your car lands in deep water and floats, how do you escape?
cards.back: If your car lands in deep water and stays afloat, escape through a window right away, since opening a door lets water rush in.

cards.front: What should you do if your car sinks?
cards.back: A sinking car usually goes down front first, leaving an air pocket in back; breathe there and escape through a window once it settles.

cards.front: What should you do if smoke comes from under the hood?
cards.back: For smoke from under the hood, pull off and turn off the ignition, and smother any fire with an extinguisher, dirt or sand, never water.

cards.front: How do you prevent and handle overheating?
cards.back: In slow traffic, shifting to neutral and briefly racing the engine during stops helps prevent overheating; if steam appears, pull over, shut off the engine and do not open the radiator cap.

cards.front: What should you do if your headlights fail?
cards.back: If headlights fail, try the parking lights and turn signals; on a dark empty road, slow down on the pavement before moving onto the shoulder.

cards.front: What should you do if wipers fail or the hood flies up?
cards.back: If wipers fail in heavy rain or snow, or the hood flies up, slow down, look out the open side window, and get off the highway.

cards.front: What can you do if the accelerator sticks?
cards.back: A stuck accelerator may come free if you hook your toe under the pedal and lift; otherwise turn off the engine to slow down.

recap_hooks.text: Never outdrive your headlights, dim within five hundred feet of oncoming cars and two hundred feet behind, and use headlights from sunset to sunrise.
Look to the right edge for glare, pull well off and stay with the car in a breakdown, and slow down at night.
On snow or ice stopping takes three to twelve times as far, so start gently, brake gently, and turn on headlights with your wipers.
Do not brake in a skid; ease off in rear-wheel drive, touch the gas in front-wheel drive, and release the gas when hydroplaning.
Use low beams in fog, pull off if you cannot see, never coast in neutral, and get fresh air at the first sign of carbon monoxide.
After a blowout, lost wheel or steering failure ease off the gas, and pump a sinking brake pedal before using the parking brake.
Stay on the shoulder and slow before easing back, pull right for a car in your lane, and walk toward a train if your car is stuck.
